## Overview

Backpressure is a flow-control mechanism in streaming or async pipelines that prevents a fast producer from overwhelming a slow consumer. Rather than allowing an unbounded buffer to accumulate items until the system runs out of memory, backpressure creates a feedback loop: the consumer signals to the producer that it cannot keep up, and the producer reduces or pauses its emission rate accordingly.

## Common Implementations

### Bounded Queues

The producer writes items to a shared queue with a fixed maximum size. Once the queue reaches capacity, the producer's write operation **blocks** until the consumer drains some items, freeing space. This is straightforward but can cause the producer thread to stall.

### Credit-Based Flow Control

The consumer maintains a "credit" counter indicating how many items the producer is allowed to send. The producer may only emit an item if it has available credit. When the consumer processes an item, it replenishes the producer's credit, granting permission to send more. This is common in message brokers and network protocols.

### Reactive-Pull Model

Instead of the producer pushing items to the consumer, the consumer **pulls** items on its own schedule. The consumer requests N items from the producer when it is ready to process them. The producer has no choice but to honor this demand model, making it naturally self-regulating. This is the basis of reactive streams patterns (e.g., Reactive Extensions, Project Reactor, RxJava).

## Why It Matters

Without backpressure:
- Buffers can grow unbounded, consuming all available memory.
- The system crashes with out-of-memory errors rather than gracefully degrading.
- Resource utilization is uneven: the producer may run at full speed while the consumer starves.

With backpressure:
- Memory usage remains bounded.
- The system self-regulates: fast producers pause when consumers cannot keep up.
- Resource utilization is more balanced and predictable.
